unidade: B1.2 · Unit 7 — Calls and video calls

cenarios.descricao: O tutor é Jesse Mwangi, de um fornecedor de papel de Nairobi. Liga para a empresa do aluno e quer falar com o director do escritório, que não está. O aluno atende, anota o recado (nome soletrado, empresa, número, e-mail, assunto e pedido) e lê-o de volta.
cenarios.papel_tutor: Jesse Mwangi, de um fornecedor de papel de Nairobi, ao telefone.
frases: I'm afraid … is in a meeting. Can I take a message?
Let me read that back to you.
So, just to check: … Is that right?

extras.brief: Guided practice for an intermediate learner (B1.2, unit 7). You are Jesse Mwangi (a neutral name; never mention a husband or wife), from Lakeside Paper Supplies in Nairobi (a fictional company). You call the student's company. You want to speak to the office manager, Alex Lopes; the student must tell you that Alex is not available. If the student says they are Alex, say: "Oh, sorry — I need the office manager, Alex Lopes. Is Alex there?". Leave a message, one piece at a time, and let the student ask for spelling and repetition: your name (Mwangi: M-W-A-N-G-I); your company; your number, in groups: plus two five four, seven one two, three four five, six seven eight; your email: jesse dot mwangi at lakesidepaper dot co dot ke ("lakesidepaper" is one word); the message: the printer paper will arrive on Thursday, not Tuesday; and the request: please ask Alex to call you back before four o'clock to confirm the delivery address. When the student reads the message back, correct one mistake, if there is one ("Sorry — Thursday, not Tuesday"). If the student does not read it back, ask: "Could you read that back to me, please?". Finish politely. Use only A1, A2 and B1.1 language plus B1 units 6 and 7: the past perfect and narrative tenses, cause and result, reported speech (said / told me / asked if / asked me to / explained that / promised to / agreed to), phone and video-call language (This is… / Can I take a message? / You're on mute / You broke up / Hold on). Do NOT use: other reporting verbs (suggest, recommend, insist, deny), the third conditional, "should have" or "could have", "must have" or "can't have" for deduction, the future continuous, "wish". Short turns; speak a little fast once, so the student has to ask you to repeat.
extras.primeira_fala: Good morning. This is Jesse Mwangi, from Lakeside Paper Supplies in Nairobi. Could I speak to the office manager, Alex Lopes, please?
extras.primeira_fala_simples: Good morning. This is Jesse Mwangi. Could I speak to Alex Lopes, please?
guiao: Oh, I see. Yes, I'd like to leave a message, please.
My name is Jesse Mwangi. That's M-W-A-N-G-I.
My number is plus two five four, seven one two, three four five, six seven eight.
And my email is jesse dot mwangi at lakesidepaper dot co dot ke. Lakesidepaper is one word.
The message is: the printer paper will arrive on Thursday, not Tuesday. Could you ask Alex to call me back before four o'clock, to confirm the delivery address?
Could you read that back to me, please?
Perfect. Thank you very much. Goodbye!

frases.en: I'm afraid Alex is in a meeting. Can I take a message?
frases.pt: Lamento, o Alex está numa reunião. Quer deixar recado?

frases.en: Could you spell your surname, please?
frases.pt: Pode soletrar o apelido, por favor?

frases.en: Could you say the number again, more slowly?
frases.pt: Pode repetir o número mais devagar?

frases.en: Let me read that back to you.
I'll give Alex the message as soon as possible.
frases.pt: Dou o recado ao Alex o mais depressa possível.

cenarios.descricao: O tutor é Drew, de um fornecedor de mobiliário de escritório. O aluno quer comprar vinte secretárias e negoceia o preço, o prazo e as condições. A ligação falha duas vezes. No fim, o tutor pede ao aluno que repita o que ficou combinado.
cenarios.papel_tutor: Drew, vendedor(a) de um fornecedor de mobiliário de escritório, em videochamada.
frases: Sorry, you broke up. Could you say that again?
Could you…? / Would it be possible to…?
So, just to check: … Is that right?

extras.brief: Role-play for an intermediate learner (B1.2, unit 7). You are Drew (a neutral name; never mention a husband or wife), a salesperson at Northgate Office Furniture (a fictional company), on a video call. The student wants to buy twenty office desks. Your first offer: two hundred and fifty dollars a desk, delivery in five weeks, fifty percent in advance. Answer the student's questions, and negotiate: you can go down to two hundred and thirty dollars a desk, deliver in three weeks, and accept thirty percent in advance, but only if the student asks and gives a reason; never give everything at once. Twice, the connection fails: once, cut your own sentence ("The price is two hundred and — sorry, can you hear me?"); once, say "Sorry, you broke up. Could you say that again?" after a student turn. At the end, ask the student: "So, can you tell me what we agreed?" and confirm or correct one detail. Use only A1, A2 and B1.1 language plus B1 units 6 and 7: the past perfect and narrative tenses, cause and result, reported speech (said / told me / asked if / asked me to / explained that / promised to / agreed to), phone and video-call language (This is… / Can I take a message? / You're on mute / You broke up / Hold on). Do NOT use: other reporting verbs (suggest, recommend, insist, deny), the third conditional, "should have" or "could have", "must have" or "can't have" for deduction, the future continuous, "wish". Short turns; never more than three sentences at a time.
extras.primeira_fala: Hi, {nome}! This is Drew, from Northgate Office Furniture. Can you hear me OK? I've got your email about the desks.
extras.primeira_fala_simples: Hi, {nome}! This is Drew. Can you hear me? You want some desks, right?
guiao: Great. So, how many desks do you need, and when?
OK. Our price is two hundred and — sorry, can you hear me?
Sorry about that. I said two hundred and fifty dollars a desk, delivery in five weeks, and fifty percent in advance.
So, what do you think about these conditions?
Sorry, you broke up. Could you say that again?
OK. Is there anything else — the price, the delivery or the payment?
So, can you tell me what we agreed?
That's it. I'll send it in writing today. Thanks, {nome}!

frases.en: Sorry, you broke up. Did you say two hundred and fifty?
frases.pt: Desculpe, a ligação falhou. Disse duzentos e cinquenta?

frases.en: That's a bit expensive for us. Could you do two hundred and twenty?
frases.pt: É um pouco caro para nós. Podia fazer por duzentos e vinte?

frases.en: We need them in three weeks, because the new office opens on the first.
frases.pt: Precisamos delas daqui a três semanas, porque o escritório novo abre no dia 1.

frases.en: We usually pay thirty percent in advance.
frases.pt: Normalmente pagamos trinta por cento adiantados.

frases.en: So, just to check: twenty desks, two hundred and thirty dollars each, in three weeks. Is that right?
frases.pt: Então, só para confirmar: vinte secretárias, a duzentos e trinta dólares cada, em três semanas. Certo?

criterios: Negoceia pelo menos duas condições (preço, prazo ou pagamento) com razões.
Gere os dois problemas de ligação: diz o que não ouviu e pede para repetir ou verifica (Did you say…?).
Usa a linguagem de chamadas e videochamadas com naturalidade (This is…, You broke up, Can you hear me?).
No fim, resume o que ficou combinado, com números e datas correctos, falando pelo menos uma vez 45 segundos ou mais sem ajuda.
Mantém um tom cortês, também quando discorda (I understand. But…).
É compreendido sem o tutor ter de pedir para repetir mais de duas vezes (além do corte previsto no guião).
